function.name: requests_get
function.description: Send a GET request to a specified URL to retrieve all products and branches with triangulation runs in the latest 90 days. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to send the GET request to.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The MIME types that are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request as a dictionary of header names to header values.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

days.description: The number of days to look back for triangulation runs.

end_date.description: The end date for the data retrieval period, in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'. If null, defaults to the current date.

params.description: Optional query parameters to include in the request.

auth.description: HTTP authentication credentials as a (username, password) tuple.

cert.description: Path to a certificate file to verify the peer.

cookies.description: Cookies to send with the request as a dictionary of cookie names to cookie values.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: Proxy settings as a dictionary mapping protocol names to URLs of the proxies.

stream.description: If true, the response should be streamed; otherwise, the response will be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not.

message.content:
### What “triangulation metrics” actually mean In many scientific, engineering, and GIS (geographic information systems) workflows, **triangulation** refers to the process of dividing a region into a set of non‑overlapping triangles. Typical applications include: | Domain | Why triangulate? | Common metrics | |--------|------------------|----------------| | **Geology / Seismology** | Build 3‑D models of fault planes or subsurface layers | • Number of triangles
• Average triangle area
• Aspect ratio (skewness)
• Edge length distribution | | **Computer graphics / 3‑D modeling** | Represent surfaces efficiently | • Triangle count
• Max/min/average edge length
• Surface curvature estimates | | **Surveying / Photogrammetry** | Reconstruct terrain from point clouds | • Point‑to‑triangle distance (RMSE)
• Coverage percentage
• Delaunay quality metrics | | **Finite‑Element Analysis (FEA)** | Mesh for numerical simulation | • Element quality (e.g., minimum angle)
• Aspect ratio
• Skewness
• Mesh density (elements per unit area) | | **Navigation / GPS** | Triangulate positions from multiple satellites | • Dilution of Precision (DOP)
• Horizontal/vertical DOP | #### Typical “triangulation metrics” you might see in a report or API | Metric | What it tells you | Typical units | |--------|-------------------|---------------| | **Triangle count** | How many triangles were generated | Count | | **Average triangle area** | Rough idea of mesh resolution | m² (or other area units) | | **Minimum/maximum edge length** | Extremes in element size | m (or other length units) | | **Aspect ratio** | How stretched a triangle is (ideal ≈ 1) | Dimensionless | | **Skewness** | Deviation from equilateral shape | Dimensionless | | **Root‑mean‑square error (RMSE)** | Fit quality between model and data | m (or other units) | | **Coverage** | % of target area actually meshed | % | | **Dilution of Precision (DOP)** | Accuracy of GPS triangulation | Dimensionless | | **Mesh density** | Elements per unit area | elements/m² | These metrics help you: 1. **Validate the mesh** – ensure it meets quality thresholds for your simulation or model. 2. **Compare different runs** – see how changes in parameters affect mesh quality. 3. **Track performance over time** – monitor improvements or regressions in your workflow. --- ### How the API call you mentioned fits in The function you referenced: ```python requests_get( url="https://api.example.com/triangulation", params={"days": 90, "end_date": None} ) ``` retrieves **all products and branches that have had triangulation runs in the last 90 days**. When you call this endpoint, you’ll typically get a JSON payload that includes: - **Run metadata** (run ID, start/end times, product/branch identifiers) - **Triangulation metrics** (the list above, or a subset relevant to your domain) - **Status flags** (e.g., `completed`, `failed`, `in_progress`) You can then: 1. **Filter** by product or branch to focus on a specific dataset. 2. **Aggregate** metrics across runs to compute averages or trends. 3. **Visualize** the results (e.g., plot triangle count vs. time). --- ### Quick example of interpreting a metric set Suppose you receive the following for a recent run: | Metric | Value | |--------|-------| | Triangle count | 12,345 | | Avg. area | 0.45 m² | | Min edge | 0.02 m | | Max edge | 0.15 m | | Aspect ratio | 1.12 | | RMSE | 0.03 m | Interpretation: - **12,345 triangles** gives you a sense of mesh granularity. - **Avg. area 0.45 m²** → each triangle covers roughly that area; if you need finer detail, you might want a smaller average area. - **Edge lengths** are within a reasonable range; no extreme outliers. - **Aspect ratio 1.12** is close to ideal (1), indicating good shape quality. - **RMSE 0.03 m** suggests the mesh fits the underlying data very well. If any metric falls outside your acceptable thresholds, you’d investigate the cause (e.g., poor point cloud density, incorrect parameter settings, or algorithmic issues). --- ### Bottom line **Triangulation metrics** are quantitative measures that describe the quality, resolution, and accuracy of a triangulated mesh or triangulation‑based solution. They’re essential for validating models, comparing runs, and ensuring that your data processing pipeline produces reliable results. The API you’re calling gives you access to those metrics for recent runs, enabling you to automate monitoring and reporting.
